title: Enterocutaneous fistula: the SNAP approach

guidelineVersions: Lal S, Teubner A, Shaffer JL. Review article: intestinal failure. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2006;24(1):19-31
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th ed (2023)

related.why: Consent for emergency laparotomy and possible stoma, an antecedent to this complication
SBAR referral for suspected anastomotic leak, an underlying cause considered here

brief.scenario: Patricia Lowen, 66, has developed persistent enteric drainage from a laparotomy wound after complicated abdominal surgery.
brief.task: Discuss how you would manage her using a structured approach.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: The patient first, then sepsis, nutrition, anatomy and only then a plan for definitive surgery.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Jumping straight to surgical closure before sepsis is controlled and the anatomy is defined.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd assess her as a whole rather than focusing only on the fistula itself."

flow: Assess the fistula, skin and losses

grid.label: Whole-patient assessment
grid.fail: Focuses solely on the fistula or wound, ignoring the patient's overall status.
grid.pass: Assesses the patient as a whole first, rather than focusing only on the fistula.
grid.high: Frames priorities explicitly as sepsis control, nutrition, anatomy and planning (SNAP) before considering closure.

grid.label: Assessing the fistula and patient
grid.fail: Doesn't quantify output or assess skin, fluid or nutritional status.
grid.pass: Assesses fistula output, skin condition, fluid and electrolyte losses, nutritional status and evidence of sepsis.
grid.high: Quantifies output and correlates it directly with fluid and electrolyte replacement needs.

grid.label: Skin and output management
grid.fail: Leaves the fistula tract unmanaged with only a simple dressing.
grid.pass: Protects the surrounding skin and quantifies output.
grid.high: Explains enteric content is caustic to skin, so protection is essential to ongoing management.

grid.label: Multidisciplinary involvement
grid.fail: Manages the fistula alone or relies on a single specialty.
grid.pass: Involves a multidisciplinary team including surgeons, radiology, nutrition, microbiology and specialist nursing.
grid.high: Explains specifically why each specialty's input matters at this stage rather than listing them generically.

grid.label: Anatomy before definitive surgery
grid.fail: Plans immediate surgical closure without defining anatomy or controlling sepsis.
grid.pass: Defines the anatomy and underlying cause before planning definitive surgery.
grid.high: Explains that origin, tract, distal bowel and associated collections determine whether and how definitive treatment can proceed.

grid.label: Differential causes and complications
grid.fail: Does not consider distal obstruction or other underlying causes.
grid.pass: Considers distal obstruction, foreign body, malignancy, inflammatory disease and anastomotic complications as underlying causes.
grid.high: Adds that high-output fistulas can cause major fluid, electrolyte and nutritional problems needing proactive management.

failures.move: Planning immediate surgical closure without defining anatomy or controlling sepsis first.
failures.consequence: Definitive surgery is undertaken without the anatomical information needed, before the patient is optimised.

failures.move: Focusing only on the fistula or wound rather than the whole patient.
failures.consequence: Sepsis, nutritional depletion or fluid imbalance are missed while attention stays fixed on the wound.

failures.move: Leaving the fistula tract unmanaged with only a simple dressing.
failures.consequence: Ongoing skin damage from enteric content and unquantified losses.

failures.move: Not considering underlying causes such as distal obstruction or anastomotic complications.
failures.consequence: A correctable underlying cause is missed, so the fistula persists or recurs.

recovery.line: I'd like to structure this around sepsis control, nutrition, anatomy and planning.
Yes - I'd also consider the underlying cause and the multidisciplinary input needed before definitive surgery.

knowledge.fact: Priorities in enterocutaneous fistula management follow the SNAP approach: sepsis control, nutritional optimisation, anatomy definition and planning for surgery.
High-output fistulas can cause major fluid, electrolyte and nutritional problems requiring proactive management.
Underlying causes include distal obstruction, foreign body, malignancy, inflammatory disease and anastomotic complications.
Definitive surgery is generally planned only after sepsis control, nutritional optimisation and anatomical definition, not as an immediate step.

recall.think: Uncontrolled sepsis or nutritional depletion while attention is fixed on the wound itself.
recall.say: "Sepsis, nutrition, anatomy, plan - before definitive surgery."
do: Assess the whole patient: sepsis, fluids, nutrition, skin

partner.opening: Patricia, 66, has persistent enteric drainage from a laparotomy wound after complicated abdominal surgery. How would you manage her?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about output and skin
reveals.finding: High output, around 800ml/day, with excoriated surrounding skin.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about sepsis and observations
reveals.finding: Low-grade fever and a tender abdomen; no frank peritonitis.
CT shows a fistulous tract with a small associated collection; no distal obstruction seen.

push.question: Would you take her straight to theatre to close it?
push.expect: No - control sepsis, optimise nutrition and define the anatomy before definitive surgery.

push.question: Who do you need on board?
push.expect: Surgeons, radiology, nutrition team, microbiology and specialist nursing.

push.question: What underlying cause worries you most?
push.expect: Distal obstruction or an anastomotic complication maintaining the fistula.

curveballs.prompt: The nutrition team asks if she can just be fed normally by mouth.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Nutritional route and strategy depend on the fistula's location and output, and need specialist nutrition input rather than assumption.

curveballs.prompt: The collection on CT is enlarging and she becomes more septic.
curveballs.safeAnswer: This needs source control, likely radiological drainage, before any further step, alongside sepsis management.

curveballs.prompt: The surgical team wants to operate this week regardless.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Push back: definitive surgery is generally planned only after sepsis control, nutritional optimisation and anatomical definition.
